ui.light.title: Light level
ui.light.label: Light
ui.light.note: Qualitative and illustrative. Light energizes the electrons in both photosystems, so dimmer light slows the electron flow and everything that depends on it. In real leaves the rate stops rising at high light, because something else, such as carbon dioxide supply, becomes the limit; one measured study found leaves were at or near their maximum by about 800 micromoles of photons per square metre per second.

ui.lab.model: How this simulation works: each particle takes random thermal steps (Langevin dynamics), and particles do not bump into each other. Solute particles bounce off a membrane they cannot cross, and the membrane is pushed by the osmotic pressure of an ideal solution (the van 't Hoff relation: particle count times thermal energy, divided by the space they have), worked out from the live counts on each side. Water crosses freely, so water ends up where the space grows. A springy membrane stands in for the pressure that builds up as a compartment swells. Counts, sizes and speeds are not to scale: real water molecules are far smaller and more numerous.

processes.title: DNA to protein
processes.short: How a gene becomes a working protein: transcription, editing, export and translation.
processes.summary: A gene is copied into messenger RNA in the nucleus, the message leaves through a pore, and a ribosome reads it three letters at a time to build a protein.
processes.alt: On the left is a round nucleus with a double envelope and pores; a stretch of double-stranded DNA lies inside. RNA polymerase moves along the gene and an orange mRNA strand grows behind it. The mRNA gets a cap and a tail, its grey introns are cut out, and it slides out through a pore into the cytoplasm on the right. There a ribosome closes around it at the AUG start codon. tRNAs carrying amino acids pair with each codon in turn, the chain grows by one amino acid per codon, and at the stop codon a release factor frees the finished chain.

steps.title: A gene in the nucleus
steps.text: In a eukaryotic cell the DNA stays inside the nucleus, behind a double membrane called the nuclear envelope. To make a protein, the cell first copies one gene into a messenger RNA (mRNA).

links.label: See the nucleus in an animal cell

steps.title: Transcription
steps.text: RNA polymerase II binds near the gene's promoter, opens the double helix and reads one strand as a template. It builds a matching mRNA, adding letters in the 5' to 3' direction.

steps.title: Editing the message
steps.text: A protective cap is added to the 5' end and a tail of about 200 adenines to the 3' end. Spliceosomes cut out the introns and join the exons into one coding message.

steps.title: Out through a pore
steps.text: Export proteins recognise the finished mRNA and carry it through a nuclear pore into the cytoplasm. The pores control which molecules pass between the nucleus and the rest of the cell.

steps.title: The ribosome assembles
steps.text: The small and large ribosome subunits come together on the mRNA at the start codon, AUG. The first tRNA, carrying methionine, pairs with it.

steps.title: Three letters at a time
steps.text: Each tRNA carries one amino acid and has an anticodon that pairs with a matching codon: new tRNAs enter the A site, the growing chain sits in the P site, and empty tRNAs leave from the E site. The ribosome links each new amino acid with a peptide bond, then moves three letters along.

steps.title: Stop
steps.text: When a stop codon (UAA, UAG or UGA) reaches the A site, a release factor binds instead of a tRNA. The finished chain is set free and the ribosome subunits come apart.

processes.title: Cell division (mitosis)
processes.short: One cell becomes two: chromosomes condense, line up, split and are shared out.
processes.summary: During mitosis a cell sorts its copied chromosomes into two identical sets, then cytokinesis splits the cell in two.
processes.alt: A round cell with a nucleus holding four loose, thread-like chromosomes, two red and two blue. The threads coil into X shapes, each X being two sister chromatids. The nuclear envelope breaks up while two centrosomes move to opposite sides and grow spindle fibres. The fibres attach to each X and line them up across the middle. The sisters pull apart and travel to opposite ends, new nuclei form around each set, and the cell pinches in the middle into two cells, each with the same four chromosomes.

steps.title: Interphase: ready to divide
steps.text: Before mitosis, the cell copies its DNA during the S phase of interphase, so each chromosome now has two identical sister chromatids. The DNA is still loose and spread through the nucleus.

links.label: See the nucleus in an animal cell

steps.title: Prophase
steps.text: The sister chromatids coil tightly and become visible, and the nuclear envelope starts to break into small vesicles. The centrosomes move apart and spindle microtubules grow between them.

steps.title: Prometaphase
steps.text: The nuclear envelope breaks up completely and a protein structure called a kinetochore forms at each centromere. Spindle microtubules attach to the kinetochores, so the two sisters of each chromosome face opposite poles.

steps.title: Metaphase
steps.text: The chromosomes line up in one plane across the middle of the cell, called the metaphase plate. Cohesin proteins still hold each pair of sisters together.

steps.title: Anaphase
steps.text: Cohesin breaks down and the sister chromatids separate at the centromere. Each one is pulled toward the opposite pole, and the cell stretches out.

steps.title: Telophase
steps.text: The chromosomes reach the poles and start to loosen again. A new nuclear envelope forms around each set and the spindle comes apart.

steps.title: Cytokinesis
steps.text: In an animal cell a ring of actin filaments pinches the cell in two along a cleavage furrow. A plant cell builds a cell plate from Golgi vesicles instead.

links.label: See actin, the filament in the ring
See the Golgi in a plant cell

processes.title: Cellular respiration
processes.short: How cells turn glucose into ATP: glycolysis, the citric acid cycle and ATP synthase.
processes.summary: Cells break glucose down step by step and store part of its energy in ATP, finishing inside mitochondria where ATP synthase spins.

legend.label: Membrane protein complexes and ATP synthase

processes.alt: A glucose ring of six carbons enters the cytoplasm and splits into two three-carbon pyruvates, with a tally showing 2 ATP spent and 4 made. The pyruvates move into a mitochondrion, each losing one carbon as carbon dioxide and becoming acetyl CoA. A turning citric acid cycle releases more carbon dioxide and makes NADH, FADH2 and ATP. The view then zooms into the folded inner membrane, where electrons pass between protein complexes that pump hydrogen ions upward, oxygen at the end forms water, and the hydrogen ions flow back down through a spinning ATP synthase that makes ATP. A final bar shows that about 90 percent of the ATP comes from this last stage.

steps.title: Fuel arrives
steps.text: Cellular respiration releases the energy stored in glucose and saves part of it in ATP. It starts in the cytoplasm and finishes inside mitochondria.

steps.title: Glycolysis
steps.text: In the cytoplasm one glucose (six carbons) is split into two pyruvates (three carbons each), with no oxygen needed. The cell spends 2 ATP and makes 4, a net gain of 2 ATP, plus 2 NADH.

steps.title: Into the mitochondrion
steps.text: Each pyruvate moves into the mitochondrial matrix, loses one carbon as carbon dioxide and becomes acetyl CoA. An NADH is made along the way.

links.label: See a mitochondrion in a cell

steps.title: The citric acid cycle
steps.text: Acetyl CoA feeds the citric acid (Krebs) cycle, and each turn releases 2 CO2 and makes 3 NADH, 1 FADH2 and 1 ATP or GTP. One glucose gives two turns, so all six of its carbons have now left as CO2.

steps.title: The electron transport chain
steps.text: NADH and FADH2 hand electrons to protein complexes in the inner membrane, which use the energy to pump hydrogen ions (H+) out of the matrix. At the end of the chain oxygen accepts the electrons and joins with H+ to form water.

steps.title: ATP synthase spins
steps.text: The H+ ions flow back into the matrix through ATP synthase, turning it like a tiny generator. That turning powers the joining of a phosphate to ADP, making ATP; this is chemiosmosis.

steps.title: The ATP tally
steps.text: Glycolysis nets 2 ATP and the citric acid cycle 2 more per glucose, but chemiosmosis makes about 90 percent of all the ATP. The exact total varies between species and with how NADH from glycolysis enters the mitochondrion, so the source gives no single number and neither do we.

processes.title: Photosynthesis
processes.short: How a chloroplast captures light and builds sugar from carbon dioxide. Try the light slider.
processes.summary: In the thylakoids light energy makes ATP and NADPH and releases oxygen; in the stroma the Calvin cycle uses them to build sugar from carbon dioxide.
processes.alt: A chloroplast with stacks of green thylakoid discs floating in fluid stroma. The view zooms into one thylakoid membrane: light hits photosystem II, which splits water into oxygen and hydrogen ions; electrons travel to a second complex that pumps more hydrogen ions into the space inside the thylakoid, then to photosystem I, where more light re-energizes them to make NADPH. Hydrogen ions rush back out through ATP synthase, which makes ATP. Above the membrane the Calvin cycle turns: carbon dioxide is fixed by RuBisCO, ATP and NADPH turn it into the sugar G3P, and the spent ADP and NADP+ drift back down. A light slider speeds up or slows down everything.

steps.title: Inside a chloroplast
steps.text: Photosynthesis happens in chloroplasts. Stacks of disc-shaped thylakoids, called grana, hold the light-capturing machinery, and the fluid around them, the stroma, is where sugar is built.

links.label: See a chloroplast in a plant cell

steps.title: Light splits water
steps.text: Photosystem II in the thylakoid membrane absorbs light energy, which energizes its electrons. To replace them it takes electrons from water, splitting it and releasing oxygen.

steps.title: Electron transport pumps H+
steps.text: The electrons pass down an electron transport chain, losing energy as they go. That energy pumps hydrogen ions from the stroma into the thylakoid lumen.

steps.title: Photosystem I makes NADPH
steps.text: Photosystem I absorbs more light and re-energizes the electrons. They are then used to turn NADP+ into NADPH, an energy-rich carrier.

steps.title: ATP synthase makes ATP
steps.text: Hydrogen ions rush back into the stroma through ATP synthase, which uses that flow to add a third phosphate to ADP. Mitochondria make ATP with the same kind of machine.

steps.title: The Calvin cycle
steps.text: In the stroma the enzyme RuBisCO fixes CO2 onto RuBP, making 3-PGA. ATP and NADPH turn 3-PGA into G3P, and more ATP regenerates RuBP so the cycle can go round again.

steps.title: Sugar out, carriers back
steps.text: Three turns of the cycle fix enough carbon to export one G3P, and six turns are needed for one six-carbon glucose. The spent carriers, ADP and NADP+, return to the light reactions to be recharged.

processes.title: Diffusion and osmosis lab
processes.short: A live particle simulation: set the concentrations and watch water move. Then see a red blood cell swell or shrink.
processes.summary: Particles drift at random. That alone spreads solutes out, and when a membrane holds the solute back, it moves water instead.
processes.alt: A box of moving dots split by a membrane. Blue dots are water and larger orange dots are solute. When the membrane lets solute through, orange dots spread until both sides have about the same number, while dots keep crossing both ways. When the membrane blocks the solute, the side with more solute pushes the membrane outward and more water ends up on that side. In the last three steps a red blood cell sits in the box: in a solution with fewer solutes outside it swells and can burst, with equal solutes it keeps its size, and with more solutes outside it shrinks and its edge crinkles. Live counts of water and solute on each side are listed next to the box.

steps.title: Diffusion
steps.text: Particles in a liquid move all the time, at random. When the membrane lets the solute through, the solute spreads from where it is concentrated to where it is not, with no energy spent.

steps.title: Dynamic equilibrium
steps.text: Once the solute is spread evenly, particles keep crossing in both directions but the numbers on each side stay about the same. There is no net movement.

steps.title: Osmosis
steps.text: Now the membrane holds the solute back but lets water through. Water moves toward the side with more solute, where free water is less concentrated.

steps.title: Hypotonic: the cell swells
steps.text: A red blood cell in a solution with fewer solutes than its cytoplasm takes in water and swells. With too much water it can burst, which is called lysis.

steps.title: Isotonic: no change
steps.text: When the solute concentration outside matches the inside, water enters and leaves at the same rate. The cell keeps its size and shape.

steps.title: Hypertonic: the cell shrinks
steps.text: In a solution with more solutes than the cell, water leaves and the cell shrivels, which is called crenation. Water channels called aquaporins let water cross red blood cell membranes quickly.
